_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 4 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 2 Predict and Compare. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order (predicting a loop; the stairs loop; folding a repeat; comparing algorithms; the purpose decides; shorter is not the same as better). Robo's routes are walked with the kit's own rules (ART.robo and ART.algo.expandLoop) rather than a copy, and the two computed comparison rounds come from ART.algo.best, so the film and the lesson cannot disagree about where Robo lands or which route wins.
title: Predict and Compare
subtitle: Grade 4 Computing
objectives: Predict the outcome of algorithms that contain repetition.
Understand that the use of repetition can make algorithms more concise.
Compare and contrast algorithms designed for the same task to determine which produces the outcome that is best suited to the purpose.

beats.say: Robo's program says repeat two times, forward, forward. Where will it stop?
Work it out before you press Go. Then compare three ways to school.
Robo starts at the bottom, facing up. The flower is four squares away.
The program is short: repeat two times, then forward, forward.
To predict where it stops, unroll the loop in your head.
Do the body twice, and it unrolls to four forwards in a row.
Tap that square, then press Go. Robo runs and lands on the flower.
Loop two is longer: repeat three times, forward, turn right, forward, turn left.
Keep track of which way Robo faces. A turn changes the next forward.

at.turn: A turn changes the next forward

beats.say: One time round: forward up, turn right, forward along, turn left.
That is one up and one along. Each time round climbs like stairs.
Three times round is three up and three along: Robo reaches the school.
Making four pancakes, written out long, is twenty-two steps.
Mix the batter. Then pour, cook, flip, cook, plate.
Those five steps happen again for every pancake. Four times over.
Write them once inside repeat four times, then serve at the end.
Twenty-two steps become seven. Repetition makes an algorithm concise.
Change one step inside the loop, and every pancake changes.
Three algorithms, one task: get from home to school.
The short cut is four steps and twelve minutes, but muddy when wet.
The bus is six steps and eight minutes, warm and dry, but it costs money.
The main road is five steps and fifteen minutes. Free, and no mud.
Compare them on four things: steps, time, cost and outcome.
Comparing finds what is the same. Contrasting finds what is different.

at.same: Comparing finds what is the same

beats.say: There is no best algorithm on its own. The purpose decides.
For the fewest steps to remember, the short cut wins.
For getting there quickest, the bus. For staying dry, the bus again.
For no money and no mud, the main road. Read the purpose every time.

at.money: For no money and no mud

beats.say: It is tempting to pick the shorter algorithm.
Shorter only wins if it still does the whole job.
An algorithm that leaves a step out is shorter and wrong.
So check the purpose first. Then compare steps, time and cost.
Unroll a loop in your head, and predict where it ends.
Repetition written once makes a long algorithm concise.
Compare and contrast the algorithms, then choose for the purpose.
